works.abstract: The Fine Print of Microalgal Biofuels I want to point out what I believe to be an argumentative flaw commonly encountered in the literature on the use of algae for the production of biofuels, namely, the tendency to bundle all species and all strains of microalgae into a single entity of interest to biotechnology. Although this might seem innocuous on the surface, it has deep implications when used to encourage the development of microalgal chemicals, and biofuels in particular. Microalgae, as a group, hold great potential for commercializing a variety of products, including hydrocarbons, and should continue to be investigated from the perspective of industrial biotechnology. But to say that microalgae, again as a group, will solve the world's energy problems is at odds with the principles of process engineering and design, which must be obeyed when attempting to bring the aforementioned potential into tangible fruition. Nevertheless, various scientific and non-scientific sources substantiate algae's potential by citing their high oil content, their fast growth rate, their high photosynthetic efficiency, their ability to grow in saline or brackish water, their capacity to fix gases that are considered emissions, their ease of separation from water by methods unavailable to many other microbes, their ability to produce fine chemicals that could subsidize the cost of production, etc. (Duffy et al., 2009; Pollack, 2010; Schmidt, 2012; Wald, 2008; Wijffels and Barbosa, 2010). Furthermore, there are methodical and comprehensive analyses that study the design and economics of such processes, based on the same premises, the results of which are often used to tout the promise of microalgal biofuels. By leaving the species unspecified, however, the assumptions used in those analyses are for the most part plainly inaccurate. To the untrained reader, the claims might appear completely justifiable. After all, there are algal species that can survive in salt concentrations of 5 M (e.g., Dunaliella spp.) (Evans and Kates, 1984), species that have productivities of 30 g/m2/day (e.g., Chlorella vulgaris) (Hirano et al., 1997), species that show hydrocarbon contents above 50% (e.g., Botryococcus braunii) (Metzger and Largeau, 2005), species that produce valuable chemicals (e.g., Haematococcus spp.) (Lorenz and Cysewski, 2000), species that can be induced to autoflocculate (e.g., Scenedesmus dimorphus) (Sukenik and Shelef, 1984), among others. But to consider a process based on these assumptions, which have never been reported in the same strain, naturally-occurring or genetically modified, and to evaluate the economics of biofuel production based on these assumptions, strains credulity. As an analogy, lignocellulosic ethanol could probably be a widespread product today if one could design and build a process that used a microbe with the growth rate of Escherichia coli, the ethanol tolerance of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the thermophilic nature of Sulfolobus acidocaldarius, and the cellulolytic activity of Trichoderma reesei. I do not (and cannot) refute that an "ideal" microalgal strain harboring an optimal combination of traits could be potentially found or even engineered, but that is yet to happen. Unfortunately, those strongly supporting microalgae are all too familiar with this line of reasoning, which is similarly employed when describing the location where a potential facility would be built. There are places in the world with sufficient year-round levels of sunlight, that are close to plenty of water, in the vicinity of carbon intensive industries that can supply inexpensive CO2, and with developed road and rail networks that can support distribution of the raw materials and end products. But by no stretch of the imagination are these locations commonplace. Alarmed by the prevalence of this logic, I believe it to be essential that the readers and reviewers of such studies stop ignoring the commonsensical notion that "the devil is in the details." The potential of microalgal biofuels will be realized only if we address ways to solve the problems that are raised when those details are considered, and not brushed off as unimportant. The Problems With Algal Fuels… Production of algal oil and its conversion to useable fuels has been demonstrated repeatedly (Chisti, 2010, 2012; Chisti and Yan, 2011), but commercial production remains elusive. Algal fuels are expensive, but this will change as the technology develops. Economic competitiveness of course does not mean an environmentally sustainable production, or an ability to produce at a sufficiently large scale to meaningfully displace petroleum fuels. Microalgae are photosynthetically more efficient compared with land plants (Chisti, 2010, 2012); nevertheless, algal oil places unsustainable demands on freshwater and fertilizers as the scale of production is increased (Pate et al., 2011). Insufficiency of low-cost concentrated CO2 is a major impediment to production of algal fuels at any substantial scale (Pate et al., 2011). Producing a ton of algal biomass requires a minimum of 1.83 tons of CO2 (Chisti, 2007), but this needs to be at a concentration that is at least 100-fold greater than the concentration in the ambient atmosphere. Fossil fuel burning power plants are the main potential sources of concentrated CO2. In 2011, the US power plants emitted 2,209 MT of CO2. No more than 10% of this is likely to be accessible for producing algal biomass, as an emitting facility must be in a climatic region suitable for growing algae and have nearby the necessary land and water resources required for algal culture. If no other resource limits production, the available CO2 could be used to produce at most 120.7 MT of algal biomass. Assuming a fairly consistently attainable oil content of 40% by weight in the biomass (Chisti, 2012), nearly 48.3 MT of algal crude oil could be produced. In terms of energy content, a barrel of petroleum roughly equates to 1.25 barrels of crude algal oil (Chisti, 2012). Assuming an oil density of 887 kg m−3, as for palm oil, 48.3 MT of algal crude is equivalent to 273.9 million barrels of petroleum, or around 14.5 days of US petroleum consumption. Mechanisms for concentrating CO2 from the dilute levels in the atmosphere for supplying to algal cultures would be necessary for algal fuels to have any hope of displacing petroleum derived fuels to a level of >5%. Algal biomass contains roughly 1.2% phosphorous (P) by weight. Producing 120.7 MT of biomass as constrained by the supply of CO2, will require nearly 3.7 MT of P, or around 2.5-fold the current US production for agriculture. Therefore, methods of recycling P would be necessary for producing algal fuels. Similarly, producing 120.7 MT of algal biomass will require >85% of the current US consumption of fixed nitrogen (N) to be diverted from agriculture to growing algae. Clearly, nutrient recycling is a key requirement for sustainable production of algal fuels. An alternative is to engineer algae to fix nitrogen. Until an ability to fix nitrogen is engineered, a recycling of nitrogen through anaerobic digestion of residual algal biomass will be necessary for sustainable production of algal fuels. Anaerobic digestion is essential also for recycling the phosphorous. Production of algal fuels requires fossil energy. Substantially more energy must be recovered in the fuel compared to the fossil energy used in its production. In short, the energy ratio of the fuel must substantially exceed unity. Preferably, the energy ratio should be 8, or more, as is possible to achieve for bioethanol derived from sugarcane (Chisti, 2008). Estimates suggest an energy ratio of <1 for algal fuels in many cases. Energy ratio may be improved by reducing the energy requirements of growing the algae (Sompech et al., 2012), harvesting the biomass, extracting the oil and processing it to useable fuels; recovering energy from the spent biomass by anaerobic digestion; and improving the efficiency of photosynthesis via genetic and metabolic engineering (Stephenson et al., 2011). Advances are being made in all these areas. In nutrient sufficient conditions, the productivity of algae is severely constrained by the design of the culture system. Existing commercial outdoor ponds located in some of the most suitable climates can achieve a maximum annual averaged biomass productivity of only around 86.7 tons per hectare per year (Chisti, 2012). This productivity is much lower than what is biologically possible for algae (Chisti, 2012). This low level of productivity is mostly a consequence of the inability of sunlight to penetrate most of the volume of a culture pond (Chisti, 2012). A practical upper limit to algal oil productivity of conventional raceways is about 37,000 L/ha year (Chisti, 2012). Estimates of the theoretical maximum productivity of algal crude oil (Weyer et al., 2010) suggest that there is much scope for improving the observed productivity. Genetic and metabolic engineering will be essential for sustainable production of algal fuels, for example, by: increasing the photosynthetic productivity of the biomass and oils; modifying the oil profile and quantity produced per cell; enabling oil release from the cell into the culture broth; improving the penetration of sunlight in an algal suspension; and enhancing the ability of the cells to withstand an elevated salinity. All this is potentially feasible without too high a metabolic cost. Genetic and genomic methods are already being applied to improve production and recovery of algal fuels (Waltz, 2009), although much remains to be done in all the key areas. In summary, production of sufficient algal oil to displace about 5% of the total annual US petroleum consumption is potentially feasible if the inorganic nutrients are recycled, energy is recovered from the spent biomass, the CO2 supply bottleneck is overcome, and the cost of producing the algal biomass with an oil content of ≥40% is reduced to about $0.25/kg on a dry basis (Chisti, 2012). All this may be possible with sustained research and development spanning many years. Microalgae for Biofuels and Animal Feeds This viewpoint addresses only autotrophic microalgal biomass production using sunlight and CO2 for production of commodities, biofuels and animal feeds. Microalgae biomass, about 15,000 tons worldwide, is produced commercially almost exclusively in open ponds, mostly of the raceway paddle wheel mixed design. The main microalgae species currently produced (>90% of total) are Spirulina (Arthrospira platensis, about 10,000 tons) and Chlorella (Chlorella vulgaris, about 4,000 tons), cultivated in several dozen plants, ranging from several tens to a few thousand tons annual capacity. China accounts for approximately two-thirds of total world production, which is sold mainly for human nutritional products, with bulk (plant gate) selling prices for Spirulina and Chlorella spray-dried biomass of typically $10–25/kg and $20–40/kg, respectively. Dunaliella salina and Haematococcus pluvialis, sources of carotenoids (beta-carotene and astaxanthin, respectively), are also produced commercially, but in much smaller amounts (a few hundred tons of biomass total), and selling for much higher prices. In brief, currently produced microalgae biomass, mostly for human nutritional products, is several orders of magnitude smaller in production scale and higher in costs than required for the production of biofuels or commodity feeds, the aim of most of the hundreds of start-up companies, research consortia and university projects formed world-wide in the past decade. These currently employ an estimated ten thousand researchers and engineers, generating hundreds of patents and publications annually. A review of biofuels production by Chisti (2007), cited over a thousand times in the literature, states that closed photobioreactors (PBRs—tubes or panels outdoors or inside greenhouses, etc.) are superior to open ponds in productivity, culture purity, higher cell densities (thus lower harvesting costs), and even overall economics, and thus are the preferred production systems for biofuels and other microalgae commodities. Indeed many, even most, researchers in the algal biofuels field favor PBRs over open ponds (e.g., Wijffels and Barbosa, 2010). However, gas exchange requirements (CO2 in and O2 out) in such reactors limit individual growth units to ∼100 m2, compared to >10,000 m2 for raceway type mixed ponds (Weissman et al., 1988). Even without considering capital costs, this makes any type of closed PBR for commodities production impractical, as several hundred hectares would be required for economics of scale, requiring operating and cleaning thousands of individual PBRs compared to just a few score open ponds. About a dozen commercial PBR systems (∼1 ha) have been built over the past two decades, at costs almost 100-times higher than open ponds, but almost all failed within a few months to years. Only one system, a closed tubular PBR in Israel, currently operates commercially, producing high value (>$100,000/t) H. pluvialis biomass. Further, PBRs have overall no real advantages over ponds in terms of productivity, if based on the actual area occupied by the PBRs, their water or energy consumption, or even long-term resistance to contamination. PBRs will be used for small scale seed cultures, but at ∼0.1% of the total system size is not a major cost factor in large-scale biomass production. Productivity, tons of dry organic matter or biofuels produced per hectare in 1 year (t/ha year), is, a central issue in this field, with many literature projections based on theoretical calculations or that often exceed year or year (Chisti, et al., 2011).
